summary.text: The difference of two squares is an identity that is one of the most commonly used in mathematics.
It can be pictured as the difference of two square areas in a plane.
Used in reverse, it removes square roots from denominators and gives complex fractions real denominators.

facts.label: Proof use
facts.value: It gives a simple proof of the AM–GM inequality in two variables

facts.label: Geometric picture
facts.value: The shaded gap between two square areas, a² − b²

facts.label: Complex numbers
facts.value: It finds linear factors of a sum of two squares

facts.label: Odd squares
facts.value: The difference of two odd perfect squares is a multiple of 8

facts.label: Galileo's law
facts.value: A falling object covers 3, 5, 7 times the first distance

items.prompt: A fraction has a complex number in its denominator. How does the identity, used in reverse, help clear it?

options.label: Multiply top and bottom by the complex conjugate to get a real denominator
Add the complex conjugate to the top of the fraction only
Square the top and the bottom of the fraction
Take the absolute value of the top of the fraction

items.explain: The two factors are complex conjugates, so used in reverse the identity turns a complex number into a real one, which gives real denominators in complex fractions.

items.prompt: A fraction has a square root combined with another number in its denominator. Which trick can move the square root out of the denominator?

options.label: Add the same number to the top and the bottom
Take the square root of the numerator too
Multiply top and bottom to make a difference of two squares
Square the whole fraction and then simplify

items.explain: The identity can be used in reverse to rationalise irrational denominators, which removes surds from expressions or at least moves them.

items.prompt: A large square sheet has a smaller square sheet cut away, and the leftover shaded shape is measured. In algebra, what does the leftover area represent?

options.label: The sum of the two square areas
The gap between the two square areas
The product of the two side lengths
The perimeter of the large square

items.explain: The shaded part in the diagram represents the difference between the areas of the two squares.

items.prompt: Which well-known inequality gets a simple proof from this identity when only two variables are involved?

options.label: Mantel's theorem about triangle-free graphs
The fundamental theorem of arithmetic
Newton's method for differentiable functions
The inequality of arithmetic and geometric means

items.explain: Among its many uses, the identity gives a simple proof of the AM–GM inequality in two variables.

items.prompt: A ball dropped from rest, with no air resistance, covers some distance during the first second. In the next second, compared with the first, how far does it go?

options.label: The same distance
Twice as far
Three times as far
Four times as far

items.explain: Galileo's law of odd numbers says the object covers 3, 5, 7 and so on times its first distance in successive equal time intervals.

items.prompt: What kind of coefficients let the identity split a sum of two squares into linear factors?

options.label: Whole-number coefficients
Negative coefficients
Fractional coefficients
Complex number coefficients

items.explain: The difference of two squares can find the linear factors of a sum of two squares using complex number coefficients.
